posts.heading: October 4, 2026
posts.text:
October 4 registered 283 feeder visits across 22 species, a slightly quieter day than the previous week's average of 312 visits and 20 species. Regulars like the Eastern Towhee, Carolina Wren, and Tufted Titmouse held steady, with the Towhee accounting for the bulk of audio detections and the Titmouse leading visual visits. Woodpeckers including Downy, Northern Flicker, Pileated, and Red-bellied individuals were recorded among the 20 species heard.

Species diversity remained high, with the Eastern Screech-Owl heard once near the end of the day and a Palm Warbler detected for the first time at this station. Several consistent species from the past week, including the Mourning Dove, Brown Thrasher, and Ruby-throated Hummingbird, were absent today. The Carolina Chickadee visited both the tube feeder and treat bowl.

Eastern Towhee detections peaked between noon and 3:00 PM, while Northern Cardinals were most active in the early morning and evening. Visual records spanned from a Northern Cardinal seen 11 minutes before sunrise to a Tufted Titmouse 32 minutes before sunset. Temperatures stayed near 22.6 C with no precipitation.

posts.heading: October 3, 2026
posts.text:
The day was quieter than the past week's average, with 292 feeder visits and 17 species recorded compared to weekly means of 311 visits and 20.6 species. Regulars such as the Tufted Titmice, Carolina Chickadees, and Carolina Wren remained consistent, while Ruby-throated Hummingbirds, Rose-breasted Grosbeaks, and American Goldfinches were absent.

A woodpecker brick was installed on the cage feeder on Thursday. The Downy Woodpecker was seen and heard twice on this day, and the Pileated Woodpecker, typically present three days a week, did not visit.

Northern Cardinals were seen both early in the morning, 12 minutes before sunrise, and late in the evening, 2 minutes after sunset. The Red-shouldered Hawk was heard five times, a regular presence that was also recorded every day in the previous week.

posts.heading: October 2, 2026
posts.text:
The station recorded 24 species and 323 visits, exceeding the previous week's average of 19.4 species and 303.6 visits. Tufted Titmice and Carolina Chickadees dominated the audio detections while also logging significant visual visits. The White-eyed Vireo returned after 12 days away, and the Brown Thrasher was recorded for the third time in the last week. The Eastern Screech-Owl provided a single pre-dawn detection at 02:00.

The station installed a cage-feeder on October 1 and refilled the seed-feeder on September 30. A second microphone was added on September 26.

posts.heading: September 29, 2026
posts.text:
The station recorded 21 species and 319 feeder visits, a count slightly lower than the seven-day average but with higher species diversity than several recent days. Eastern Towhies, Carolina Chickadees, and Tufted Titmice dominated the counts, with the latter leading in visual sightings.

The audio log captured 18 heard species compared to 11 seen. This increase is linked to the second microphone, c120-extra, which began operating last week. Red-shouldered Hawks and Eastern Phoebes were frequent in the audio feed despite lower visibility.

American Goldfinches and Brown Thrashers returned to the station after more than ten days away. The Downy Woodpecker, present in the last few days, was absent today. With no new species and feeder refills from late in the week still in effect, the station maintained steady activity from familiar birds.

posts.heading: September 28, 2026
posts.text:
The station recorded 389 feeder visits and 20 species, both figures exceeding the weekly averages of 289 visits and 17.7 species. This marked a busier day than any of the previous six, with only Monday approaching the species count, though Monday had fewer visits. Regulars including the Carolina Chickadee, Carolina Wren, and Northern Cardinal were consistently heard and seen, maintaining their presence through the week.

Audio detections included a Northern Flicker and a Chipping Sparrow, each registered as a first-time record for the station. These detections occurred after the second microphone began listening on September 26, so they reflect the new audio source rather than new arrivals. No other species were heard for the first time, and no new visual firsts were recorded.

The Ruby-throated Hummingbird, which appeared each of the prior seven days, was not detected today. Station changes over the week included a seed and nectar feeder refill on Friday and the addition of the second microphone on Saturday.
